newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee ends up, but Brazil freeze unlikely.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee ends up, but Brazil freeze unlikely.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures ended sharply higher on Monday, as weather forecasts calling for another chilly night in top-grower Brazil sparked a rash of speculative buying, traders said.

"The weather did it, although no one is predicting a freeze," said PaineWebber analyst Bernard Savaiko. "It looked like emotionally charged spec buying. But it is probably a covenient excuse to get out of shorts, and I think it is scaring shorts out rather than attracting more longs."

July arabicas surged 16.05 cents per lb -- or nearly seven percent -- on the day, to 253.30 cents, after ranging between 256.00 and 235.50 cents. Second-month September jumped 9.45 cents, to 223.60 cents, while the back months closed up 7.25 to 9.00.
The July/September spread, a barometer of near-term availability, bulged to 29.70 cents today from 23.10 cents on Friday.

Although Brazil's coffee regions escaped damaging cold this past weekend, traders said reports of frost in low-lying areas where no coffee is grown were enough to rattle nerves with memories of two severe frosts three years ago still fresh. The 1994 frosts -- one in June and another in July -- damaged coffee trees and sent futures prices spinning higher.
On Monday, Brazilian forecasters are anticipating cold temperatures again in the region early tomorrow morning and a repeat of frosts in the lower regions where coffee is not grown.

But Smith Barney meterologist Jon Davis said that the airmass, which produced the cold weather this weekend, is in the process of moving out into the Atlantic and will bring in warmer weather during the next week.

"In fact, during the next week there is no indication of any significant cold airmasses moving up into Brazil from Argentina," Davis stated in his daily weather update. "Thus, there is no threat of any frost/freeze damage during the next week in Brazil."
While PaineWebber's Savaiko generally brushed aside weather concerns, he said a more worrying development for the market was the divergence in prices between arabica and robusta beans.
"I am more troubled by the differential between London and New York," he said. "It is too tempting for roasters to alter their blends."

Market participants also noted the spread between the price of Brazilian beans and other mild coffees, which is likely to prompt some substitution and help ease tight supplies of higher quality arabica beans.
After Monday's close, the CSCE said certified coffee stocks rose by 590 60-kg bags as of June 6, to 44,215 bags, There were 2,578 bags pending grading, the exchange said.
